turns.text: Every backlog drifts. Stories without acceptance criteria. Features without a parent. Sizes nobody agreed. Halyard is the product owner's mate. It reads the backlog, finds the drift, drafts the fix, and waits for a person to approve it. Nothing moves without your say.
Here is how Halyard fits together. Everything runs on one machine. A PowerShell launcher compiles the engine in memory, and the browser talks to it on localhost.
Inside the engine: review, intelligence for drafting and sizing, planning, and a proposal store. Every change starts as a proposal.
Halyard reads your backlog from GitHub, read only. The write gateway lets it write to one place: the sandbox backlog you configure.
Model calls go through Fairlead and nowhere else. Halyard's own key sits in Windows Credential Manager. The OpenAI key stays in Lazarette, shared to Fairlead.
Out the other side: four tables for Semaphore, and the weekly dashboard as an Outlook draft.
Dashed means planned: live Shellback skills, and a runner on your repositories.
One rule holds it together. Nothing is written until a person approves.
Every tool in the fleet needs a model key. At OpenAI, create a new secret key.
Name it something generic. I call mine fleet-tools. Seven days is plenty.
Copy it once. OpenAI never shows it again.
The key goes into Lazarette, the encrypted vault on this machine.
Test credential checks it against OpenAI's read-only endpoint. HTTP two hundred. The key is good.
Share it with Fairlead by name, and Fairlead sees only what you share.
Fairlead reads it from the vault and connects. Eighty-three models, in under a second.
Fairlead gives each tool its own key. Pick Halyard and install it. It lands in Windows Credential Manager.
Halyard's config file names the backlog it reads, the backlog it may write to, and the write mode. The browser can't change any of it.
Test the model. Under two seconds, end to end.
For this walkthrough we seed a synthetic backlog. Thirty items, a quarter of them with deliberate gaps.
Each one is a real GitHub issue with a run label, so the whole run comes out again in one click. It takes about two minutes, paced for the rate limits.
Thirty of thirty. The backlog is live.
The overview shows the shape of the backlog and what needs attention: items to review, missing parents, topology errors. Scroll down for the findings by severity, and the next actions.
Review checks every item against its level's definition of ready and the parent chain. Each finding names the fix that closes it.
Hierarchy shows the tree, theme to task.
Draft missing sections sends each gap to the model through Fairlead. Real model, a few seconds per item.

Six drafts, all high confidence. Each is a proposal with a reason. Open one and read the diff: the model adds what's missing and leaves the rest alone. And if it ever drops a section, Halyard puts it back word for word.
Approve the high-confidence drafts, then apply. Six written to the backlog on GitHub, and the apply is recorded.
Every apply is recorded with what it replaced. Undo previews first, then restores the earlier text. Six items restored.
Anything a person edited since is left alone. The proposals go back to pending, so approve and apply again when you're ready.
Work comes in from anywhere. A raw ticket, or a note typed straight into Intake. Two loose notes, no structure at all.
Preview the drafts. Halyard turns each note into a structured work item and copies it into the backlog, with a link back to where it started.
Plan fills the next sprints from ready stories.
Capacity comes from the team file. Owners are matched on skills, and anything that slipped last sprint goes first.
Skills come from Shellback peer cards today. A live Shellback link is planned.
Upward, Halyard drafts the portfolio story for leadership. This one is the live model, thinking.
Themes, priorities, risks and the next quarter, with the facts every claim rests on. Everything it says about the backlog, it can point to.
The leadership page puts features on track, velocity, ready backlog, capacity and blockers on one screen.
One click exports backlog health for Semaphore, as four tables ready to chart.
The weekly dashboard opens in Outlook as a draft, so a person reviews it and presses send.
Next on the chart: a runner on the team's repositories. It watches commits and pull requests, and writes the story for the work it sees.
Developers stop doing the admin. The product owner approves what the runner proposes, through the same diff and the same gate.
Production stays shut. Promote needs a production write mode, an explicit allow flag, a typed phrase and a diff, and none of it can be switched on from the browser.
The write audit lists every write Halyard made. Every one went to the backlog.
Halyard proposes. People decide. That's the watch. Fair winds.
